§0Part A · orientation

Orientation — PK vs PD

Two halves of pharmacology; this guide is the first half.

Pharmacology has two complementary questions about the drug–body interaction:

  • Pharmacokinetics (PK) — what the body does to the drug (how the body handles it).
  • Pharmacodynamics (PD) — what the drug does to the body, and how it does it.

This guide covers the PK side — specifically absorption and distribution, the first two stages of ADME (§1). The unit's LO1 is exactly this: apply core PK/PD concepts to explain drug behaviour and effects in the body.

Reasoning · why PK comes before PD

A drug can only act where it arrives, at the concentration it arrives in. PD (receptors, effects) is meaningless until you know how much drug reaches the target and when — and that is PK. So we first trace the journey: in through absorption (§3–§4), around through distribution (§5), and — later in the unit — out through metabolism and excretion.

Memory hook · PK vs PD

PK = Kinetics = the body Kicks the drug around. PD = Dynamics = the Drug Does something to the body.

§1L3 · framework

Pharmacokinetics & ADME

The drug's four-stage journey through the body.

Pharmacokinetics = pharmaco (drug) + kinetics (characterised by movement). It answers one practical question: how much drug will reach the site(s) of action, and when?

The answer is the four stages of drug disposition — ADME:

ADME — the four stages
StageWhat happens
A — AbsorptionDrug moves from the site of administration into the plasma (§3–§4).
D — DistributionDrug spreads between plasma and tissues (§5).
M — Metabolism (biotransformation)Chemical modification, largely by cytochrome P450 enzymes.
E — ExcretionDrug (and metabolites) leave the body.

Plate 1.1 shows ADME mapped onto the body.

Label Key
Absorption / Distribution
Drug enters plasma, then spreads to tissues.
Metabolism / Excretion
Biotransformation (cytochrome P450) then removal from the body.
Memory hook · ADME

Absorption → Distribution → Metabolism → Excretion. "In, around, changed, out." This guide handles A and D.

§2L3 · membranes

Drug movement across membranes

Every ADME stage is a membrane crossing — here's how molecules get through.

To be absorbed and distributed, a drug must cross cell membranes. There are a few basic mechanisms:

  • Passive transport — movement from high to low concentration, no energy: paracellular (A, between cells), simple diffusion (B, straight through the lipid), and facilitated diffusion (C, down-gradient but via a special carrier).
  • Active transport — movement against the gradient, using carriers + energy (e.g. ABC transporters).
  • Pinocytosis — fluid endocytosis (D); also internalises small particles suspended in extracellular fluid.

Plate 2.1 shows these routes across the membrane.

Label Key
Paracellular (A) · diffusion (B)
Passive routes — between cells / straight through the lipid.
Facilitated (C) · active · pinocytosis (D)
Carrier-mediated (down-gradient), against-gradient (energy), and fluid endocytosis.
Reasoning · why passive diffusion dominates

Passive diffusion dominates transmembrane movement of most drugs. It needs no carrier and no energy — any small, lipid-soluble, uncharged molecule simply dissolves through the membrane down its gradient. That single fact is why the rest of absorption (§3) is really a story about lipid solubility and ionisation: make a drug more lipid-soluble/uncharged and it crosses; make it charged and it's stuck.

§3L3 · absorption

Absorption

From the site of administration into the plasma — and what speeds it or slows it.

Absorption is the movement of drug from the site of administration into the plasma — and most drugs must be absorbed to act. In most cases ~75% of an oral drug is absorbed in 1–3 hours, but many factors change that.

Factors affecting rate & degree of absorption
Drug & physiologicalPatient
Lipid solubility (lipid:water partition coefficient) — incl. molecular weight & structure (pKa); surface area; gut content; GI transit time; blood flow to the site; drug interactionsAge, health status, genetic polymorphisms

§3.1Lipid solubility, weak acids/bases & pKa

Non-polar molecules (electrons uniformly distributed) freely cross membranes. But many drugs are weak acids or bases, so their ability to cross depends on how ionised they are — which depends on the drug's pKa and the pH around it. The pKa is the pH at which 50% of the drug is in its ionised form.

Reasoning · why ionisation controls crossing

Only the uncharged form is lipid-soluble enough to diffuse through a membrane; the charged (ionised) form is repelled by the lipid core. A weak acid gives up its proton (ionises) as pH rises; a weak base ionises as pH falls. So the same drug crosses easily in one compartment and is stuck in another — set up entirely by pKa vs local pH. (Rule of thumb: when pH < pKa the environment is acidic and the compound is mostly protonated.)

§3.2pH partition & ion trapping

Because different compartments have different pH, a drug can be ion-trapped — its equilibrium distribution shifted to one side of a membrane. Take a weak acid (pKa 4.4) between plasma (pH 7.4) and gastric juice (pH 1.4), separated by a lipid barrier: only the uncharged HA crosses and equilibrates, but on each side HA dissociates to a different extent — far more in plasma (high pH) than in gastric acid (low pH). The charged A⁻ can't cross, so the drug accumulates where it ionises most.

Plate 3.1 shows the weak-acid equilibrium across the gastric/plasma barrier.

Label Key
HA (uncharged)
The only form that crosses the lipid barrier; equilibrates across it.
A⁻ (charged)
Trapped on the side where higher pH favours dissociation (plasma vs gastric juice).
Clinical / real-world · trapping works both ways

Ion trapping is used deliberately: in aspirin (a weak acid) overdose, giving bicarbonate to alkalinise the urine ionises the drug in the renal tubule, traps it there and speeds its excretion. The same principle explains why weak acids are absorbed well from the acidic stomach (they stay uncharged there) while weak bases are not.

§3.3The Henderson–Hasselbalch relationship

Quantitatively: the stronger an acid, the greater its ionisation, the lower its pKa, and the lower the pH it produces in solution. The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation lets you calculate the unionised fraction of a drug at a given pH — i.e. how much is in the membrane-crossing form.

Plate 3.2 plots ionisation against pH for a weak acid and a weak base.

Label Key
Weak acid / weak base
% ionised changes with pH around the pKa.
Unionised fraction
The membrane-crossing form; calculated from pKa and pH.

§3.4Routes of administration

Where you put the drug shapes its absorption. The main routes:

  • Enteral / mucosal — oral (po), sublingual, rectal, and application to other epithelial surfaces (skin, cornea, vagina).
  • Inhalation — pulmonary.
  • Injection — subcutaneous (SC), intramuscular (IM), intravenous (IV), intra-arterial, intrathecal, intravitreal.

Plate 3.3 maps the routes and their first-pass behaviour.

Label Key
Oral / sublingual / rectal
Oral goes via the liver (first-pass); sublingual/rectal largely bypass it.
Inhalation / injection
Pulmonary; SC, IM, IV (bypasses absorption & first-pass), and others.
Memory hook · §3 in one line

Absorption = ADME's A, driven by passive diffusion, gated by lipid solubility & pKa/ionisation, tuned by surface area & GI transit, and chosen by the route.

§4L4 · measuring absorption

Bioavailability & PK parameters

How we measure how much drug actually gets in — and why oral so often loses.

§4.1PK parameters — AUC, Cmax, Tmax

We measure PK from concentration-versus-time data — usually the drug concentration in blood plasma (Cp), which is used in drug development and in therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) to individualise doses (other fluids — urine, saliva, CSF, milk — can be used too). Three parameters come straight off the curve:

  • AUC — area under the concentration-time curve: a measure of total drug exposure.
  • Cmax — the maximum plasma concentration reached.
  • Tmax — the time taken to reach Cmax.

Plate 4.1 shows AUC, Cmax and Tmax against the therapeutic range.

Label Key
AUC
Area under the curve = total drug exposure.
Cmax / Tmax
Peak concentration and the time to reach it, relative to the therapeutic range.

§4.2Bioavailability & first-pass metabolism

Bioavailability (F) is the fraction of a dose that proceeds unaltered from the site of administration to the systemic circulation. If 100% of the dose reaches the blood, F = 1.0; if only a fraction does, F < 1.0. Note F captures only the total fraction absorbed — it neglects the rate of absorption.

Low oral bioavailability is mainly due to first-pass metabolism and low absorption. Interindividual variability (beyond the drug preparation) comes from changes in the enzymatic activity of the gut wall or liver (first-pass), gastric pH and intestinal motility.

Plate 4.2 shows how first-pass metabolism cuts oral bioavailability.

Label Key
First pass
Gut-wall & hepatic enzymes destroy oral drug before systemic circulation.
Bioavailability (F)
Fraction surviving to the systemic blood; IV = 1.0, oral < 1.0.
Reasoning · why the route decides the loss

An oral drug is absorbed from the gut into the portal vein → liver, where gut-wall and hepatic enzymes can destroy much of it before it ever reaches the systemic circulation — the first-pass effect. IV goes straight into the systemic blood, so F = 1.0 by definition (no absorption step, no first pass). Sublingual and rectal routes drain (largely) into systemic veins that bypass the portal system, so they escape most first-pass metabolism — which is exactly why GTN for angina is given under the tongue.

Worked example · matching an oral dose to an IV dose

Q. Drug X has an oral bioavailability of ~50%. If the standard IV dose is 50 mg, how much should be given orally to achieve the same plasma exposure?
Reasoning. Only F of an oral dose reaches the blood, so oral dose × F = IV dose. Rearranged: oral dose = IV dose ÷ F = 50 mg ÷ 0.5 = 100 mg.
Answer: 100 mg (option C). The lower the bioavailability, the more oral drug you need to match an IV dose.

§5L4 · distribution

Distribution

Once in the blood, where does the drug go — and why does it matter?

Distribution is the movement of a drug throughout the body. Its equilibrium pattern between compartments is set by: permeability across tissue barriers, binding within compartments, pH partition (§3.2), fat:water partition, and blood flow to the tissue.

§5.1Body fluid compartments

50–70% of body weight is water (less in women than men), distributed across four compartments, plus fat as the large non-polar store:

  • Plasma · Interstitial fluid · Intracellular fluid
  • Transcellular fluid — cerebrospinal, intraocular, peritoneal, pleural and synovial fluids, and digestive secretions.
  • Fat — the large non-polar compartment where lipophilic drugs accumulate.

Plate 5.1 shows the compartments as a percentage of body weight; Plate 5.2 shows how a drug's properties decide which compartments it reaches.

Label Key
Plasma · interstitial · intracellular
The main water compartments (+ transcellular).
Bound vs free drug
Only free drug crosses/acts; binding holds drug in a compartment.
Label Key
Intravascular / interstitial
Where small vs large / polar drugs can reach.
Fat
Lipophilic drugs partition into the non-polar fat compartment.

§5.2Plasma protein binding

In the blood, drugs bind reversibly to plasma proteins — mainly albumin (which carries mostly acidic drugs) and α₁-acid glycoprotein (mostly basic drugs). The bound and free forms sit in equilibrium: free drug + protein ⇌ drug–protein complex. Crucially, only the free (unbound) drug exerts a pharmacological effect — the bound fraction is an inactive reservoir.

Plate 5.3 shows binding of a drug to plasma albumin.

Label Key
Bound fraction
Inactive reservoir on albumin (acidic drugs) / α₁-AGP (basic drugs).
Free fraction
Only the free/unbound drug exerts an effect.
Clinical / real-world · displacement can be dangerous

Because only free drug acts, anything that shifts the equilibrium matters. Two highly protein-bound drugs given together can displace each other from albumin, suddenly raising the free concentration of one — a classic mechanism of drug interaction and toxicity (e.g. displacing warfarin → bleeding). It also means that in low-albumin states (liver disease, malnutrition) the free fraction of bound drugs rises.

§5.3Volume of distribution (Vd)

The apparent volume of distribution (Vd) is the volume of fluid into which a drug appears to be distributed or diluted — it does not correspond to a real anatomical volume. It's calculated as:

Vd = amount of drug in the body (mg) ÷ plasma concentration (mg/L)

Vd is affected by age, gender, body composition and disease. For scale: plasma ≈ 0.05 L/kg (~4 L), extracellular fluid ≈ 0.2 L/kg, total body water ≈ 0.55 L/kg (~42 L). Examples: paracetamol Vd ≈ 65 L (1–1.2 L/kg); warfarin Vd ≈ 10 L (0.14 L/kg).

Plate 5.4 shows how the same dose gives different Vd depending on tissue binding.

Label Key
Low Vd
Minimal tissue binding → drug stays in plasma (Vd ≈ plasma volume).
High Vd
Tissue/fat binding → drug leaves plasma → large apparent volume.
Reasoning · what a big or small Vd tells you

Read Vd as "where the drug hides". A drug with minimal tissue binding stays in the plasma, so its Vd is small, close to the plasma volume — warfarin (heavily albumin-bound, ~0.14 L/kg) is the classic example. A lipophilic drug that leaves the blood for tissues and fat gives a large Vd — often bigger than the whole body's water, which is only possible because "volume" here is a ratio, not a real space. So Vd directly links lipophilicity → tissue accumulation (§5.1), and it sets the loading dose needed to fill that apparent volume.

R Recall checklist — PK: absorption & distribution
  • PK vs PD — PK = body→drug; PD = drug→body. ADME = Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism (CYP450), Excretion.
  • Membrane movement — passive (paracellular, diffusion, facilitated/carrier), active (against gradient, carrier+energy), pinocytosis. Passive diffusion dominates.
  • Absorption — site→plasma; ~75% oral in 1–3 h. Factors: lipid solubility/pKa, surface area, gut content, GI transit, blood flow; patient age/health/genetics.
  • pKa & ion trapping — pKa = pH at 50% ionised; only uncharged form crosses; charged form trapped where pH favours ionisation (weak acid: plasma vs gastric). Henderson–Hasselbalch gives the unionised fraction.
  • Routes — oral/sublingual/rectal/epithelial/inhalation/injection (SC, IM, IV, intra-arterial, intrathecal, intravitreal); sublingual & rectal bypass first-pass.
  • Bioavailability — F = fraction reaching systemic circulation; IV = 1.0, oral < 1.0 (first-pass + low absorption). Oral dose to match IV = IV ÷ F. AUC (exposure), Cmax, Tmax.
  • Distribution — compartments (plasma, interstitial, intracellular, transcellular) + fat; protein binding (albumin/acidic, α₁-AGP/basic; only free drug acts); Vd = amount ÷ Cp (apparent). Low Vd = plasma-bound (warfarin); high Vd = tissue/fat.
